IBM watsonx.data · Remote MCP

Give your AI agent a key to the lakehouse.

Eight steps, no terminal, no code. You'll find three values inside IBM Cloud, paste them into the form near the bottom, and this page hands you the exact configuration your agent needs.

Time about 10 minutes
You need an IBM Cloud login with access to the instance
Result a config file your agent reads on startup

On this page

  1. 01 Sign in
  2. 02 Resource list
  3. 03 Find the instance
  4. 04 Open the console
  5. 05 Instance details
  6. 06 Create an API key
  7. 07 Build the config

  9. — Keep it safe
01

Sign in to IBM Cloud

Go to cloud.ibm.com and log in with the account that owns your watsonx.data instance.

Working across more than one account?

The account switcher in the top header decides what you can see. Pick the account the instance lives in before moving on — otherwise it won't show up in step 3.

02

Open the Resource list

Click the menu (☰) at the top left, then choose Resource list. This is every service in the account, grouped by type. Most groups will say (0) — that's normal.

03

Expand Databases and click your instance

Scroll to Databases and click the arrow to expand it. Your watsonx.data instance is the row with watsonx.data in the Product column. Click its name.

Nothing under Databases?

Either the instance lives in a different account, or your user hasn't been granted access to it. Ask whoever administers the account to add you.

04

Open the web console

The instance page opens on the Manage tab. Click Open web console — the plain link, not the blue Launch in watsonx button next to it. A new tab opens with the dark watsonx.data console.

05

Open instance details and copy two values

In the console, click the information icon (ⓘ) in the top header — it may be labelled About. A panel slides out listing the identifiers for your instance. Scroll it.

Two rows matter. Copy both with the copy icon to the right of each — never by selecting the text.

The CRN on screen is cut short

It ends in … because the panel truncates it. The real value is much longer — it continues with the rest of the account ID plus your instance ID, and usually ends in ::. The copy icon gives you the whole thing; your eyes don't.

CRN and Instance ID are different fields. The Instance ID is the short d8aae34a-… value. It won't work here. Take the row that says Cloud resource name.

No MCP server endpoint row?

Then this instance's plan or version doesn't offer the hosted MCP server yet. Stop here and talk to your watsonx.data administrator rather than working around it.

06

Create an API key

This is how the agent proves it's you. Back in the IBM Cloud tab, open Manage in the top header and choose Access (IAM), under the "Security and access" heading.

In the IAM sidebar, click API keys (under "Manage identities"), then the blue Create button. Give the key a name you'll recognise later, like watsonx-data-mcp.

You get one chance to copy it

The key is shown once, right after you create it. Copy it or download it right away. If you lose it, delete the key and make a new one — there's no way to look it up again.

You also need the IBM ID that key belongs to. That's normally the email address you logged in with. If an administrator created the key under a service ID instead, your ID is the ServiceId-… value rather than an email.

07

Build your config

Paste your three values in. The configuration on the right fills in as you type.

This stays on your computer

Everything here runs in your browser. Nothing is uploaded, logged, or sent anywhere — you can disconnect from the network and it still works.

This builds the address below. It should match the MCP server endpoint you saw in step 5 — if it doesn't, pick a different region.

https://us-south.lakehouse.cloud.ibm.com/api/v1/watsonxdata/mcp

Your config 

          

        

      


      

        The long string after Basic is your ID and key joined together and encoded. It isn't encryption — anyone holding it holds your key.
      

    

  


  
  

    
08
Add it to IBM Bob

    

      
Your config goes in a file that the agent reads when it starts. Below is the route through IBM Bob. Other agents differ in the details but the shape is the same: find the MCP settings, open the config file, paste inside mcpServers.


      
a. Open the settings gear in the Bob panel

      
The gear (⚙) sits in the row of icons at the top right of the Bob panel, next to the ✓ and + icons.


      

      
b. Select the MCP tab

      
Bob Settings opens. Choose MCP in the left column. You'll see every MCP server Bob knows about, with a Status and a Scope.

      
The + icon to the right of the search box is how you add a server by hand — that's the one you want.


      

      
c. Open the config file and paste

      
On the MCP tab, click whichever fits:


      

        Edit Global MCP
        Edit Project MCP
      


      

      

        
Edit Global MCP~/.bob/mcp.json — every project you open in Bob

        
Edit Project MCP.bob/mcp.json — this project only. Bob creates the file if it isn't there.

      


      
Pick Global if you want the lakehouse available everywhere. Both files are JSON with an mcpServers object holding named servers.


      

        
If the file already has servers in it

        
Don't paste over the whole file. Add only the "watsonx.data-mcp-server": { … } block inside the existing mcpServers object, and put a comma between it and its neighbour.

        
If the file is empty or just {}, paste the whole thing from step 7 as-is.

      


      

        
Project MCP files get committed by accident

        
.bob/mcp.json lives inside your project, so git will offer to commit it — with your key inside. Add .bob/ to .gitignore, or use Global instead.

      


      
d. Check it worked

      
Save the file. Back on the MCP tab, hit the refresh (⟳) or restart Bob, then look at your server's row:

      
    
        
  •  Connected — you're done.
    • 
        
  •  Disabled — the server is there but switched off. Click the row to enable it.
    • 
        
  • Red dot — click the row to read the error, then see below.
    • 
      

      
Also confirm Enable MCP tools for new tasks is toggled on, and start a new task — existing tasks keep the tool set they started with, so an open conversation won't pick up the new server.

      
Then ask Bob: “are you connected to a watsonx instance?” It should come back with your region, version, plan and instance ID.


      

        
If it fails

        
401 or “unauthorized” — the ID and key pair is wrong. Check the ID is the right one for that key, and that the key wasn't truncated when you pasted it.

        
404, or connects but no tools — the CRN is incomplete or the region is wrong. Re-copy the CRN with the copy icon and confirm the address matches the MCP server endpoint on the panel.

        
Bob won't load the file — the JSON has a typo. A missing comma or brace breaks the whole file, including servers that used to work. Paste it fresh from step 7.

      


      

        
Using a different agent?

        
Claude Desktop: Settings → Developer → Edit Config. VS Code extensions: look for an mcp.json or mcp_settings.json in the extension's settings folder. Anything else: look for MCP servers, Connectors, or Tools in its settings. The config from step 7 is the same either way.

      

    

  


  
  

    
—
Keep it safe

    

      
The finished config contains a working credential to your lakehouse. Treat the file the way you'd treat a password.

      
    
        
  • Don't commit it to a repository. Not a private one either.
    • 
        
  • Don't paste it into chat, tickets, or docs. That includes pasting it to a colleague to “check the format”.
    • 
        
  • Delete the key when you're done with it, or if it's ever been somewhere it shouldn't. Manage → Access (IAM) → API keys → delete. Then make a new one and redo step 7.
    • 
        
  • Ask for a key with only the access you need. A key that can read one catalog is a smaller problem than one that can do anything.
    • 
      

      
The agent acts as you. Anything you can do in watsonx.data, it can do — including writing data.

    

  


  

    
Built for the hosted (remote) watsonx.data MCP server. Field names and panel layout can shift between releases — if a screen doesn't match, trust the screen and check the current IBM documentation.
